drills.q: Why are prefill and decode described as having opposite bottlenecks?
drills.a: Prefill processes all prompt tokens in one parallel pass, reusing each weight load across many positions -- high arithmetic intensity, compute-bound. Decode processes one token per step but reads the same weight matrices plus the whole accumulated KV cache for just that one position -- arithmetic intensity falls ~5x, making it memory-bandwidth-bound.

drills.q: Derive the KV-cache bytes/token formula and compute it for a 70B model (80 layers, GQA-8, head_dim=128, BF16).
What problem does PagedAttention solve and what's the mechanism?
drills.a: Fragmentation from contiguous per-request KV-cache allocations sized for worst-case length (60-80% waste). PagedAttention partitions the cache into fixed-size blocks with a per-sequence block table (logical->physical mapping), allocating on demand and freeing immediately on completion -- waste drops under 4%.

drills.q: Explain continuous batching and why static batching underperforms, and why continuous batching depends on PagedAttention-style memory management.
drills.a: Static batching idles finished slots until the whole batch's longest sequence completes. Continuous batching evicts/admits sequences every decode iteration, keeping utilization high. It depends on block-based (paged) allocation because adding/removing a sequence's blocks independently of every other sequence's layout would require expensive memory shuffling under naive contiguous allocation.

drills.q: What is chunked prefill, what problem does it fix, and what's the cost of making the chunk size very small?
drills.a: Splits a long prompt's prefill into fixed chunks (vLLM default 2,048 tokens) interleaved with other sequences' decode steps, fixing head-of-line blocking where one long prefill would otherwise stall everyone else's TPOT. Making chunks very small raises the long-prompt request's own TTFT (more scheduling iterations to fully ingest) and adds per-chunk scheduling overhead -- it's a tradeoff, not a free fix.

drills.q: Compare vLLM's prefix caching to SGLang's RadixAttention, and explain when vLLM's simpler approach is actually preferable.
drills.a: vLLM hashes fixed-size blocks by content and reuses exact hash matches. RadixAttention organizes the whole KV-cache pool as a radix tree, automatically discovering shared prefixes across any requests. vLLM's simpler approach is preferable on workloads with little cross-request prefix structure, where radix-tree bookkeeping overhead buys nothing.

drills.q: Define TTFT and TPOT, and explain how increasing batch size affects each plus throughput -- is there a batch size that minimizes all three?
drills.a: TTFT: queueing + prefill time, scales with prompt length/load. TPOT: memory-bandwidth-bound decode step time, scales with total KV cache read per step. Bigger batch raises throughput (better weight-load amortization) but raises TPOT (more cache read per step, more contention) and can raise TTFT for new arrivals. No single batch size minimizes all three -- it's a genuine three-way tradeoff surface; you pick the point matching your SLO.

drills.q: Your KV-cache pool fills up under load. What are your options and what does each cost?
drills.a: Reject/queue new requests (safest, adds latency for that request), preempt a running low-priority sequence (wastes compute, spikes its latency), offload cold blocks to CPU/object storage (costs fetch latency if reused), or reduce max batch/context admitted (costs throughput/capability). Real systems combine admission control with offloading rather than relying on one mechanism; naive LRU-by-recency eviction can starve high-priority requests behind a burst of low-priority ones.

drills.q: Do the cost-model arithmetic: $2.50/hr GPU, 5,000 tokens/sec aggregate throughput -- compute $/million tokens, and explain whether a bigger batch always lowers this.
drills.a: 2.50 / (5,000*3,600) * 1,000,000 ~= $0.14 per million tokens. Not always -- only up to the memory-bandwidth or KV-cache-capacity ceiling; past that, added concurrency causes preemption/queueing that can raise effective cost via wasted recomputation, and it always raises TPOT, so the cost-minimizing batch size and the latency-SLO-respecting batch size are frequently different numbers.

drills.q: Design the serving strategy for a RAG chat product: short-to-medium prompts, heavily shared system prompt/retrieved-context boilerplate, tight latency SLO.
drills.a: Prioritize prefix caching or a radix-tree-native engine (heavy prefix reuse from shared system prompt/retrieval wrapper). Use continuous batching with a moderate batch size chosen from the TPOT SLO, not maximized for throughput. Enable chunked prefill with a modest chunk size to protect TPOT when a long-context request arrives. Size the KV-cache pool from measured p99 concurrent-sequence count times typical context length, with admission control (reject/queue, not silent preemption), and monitor TTFT/TPOT/queue depth separately rather than end-to-end latency alone.
